title: How I Built Monster Legs
summary: NH recaps reaching 28-inch legs: one inch from 2020-2023 by fixing weak hamstrings while recomping, and another while gaining 10 lb. His keys were hypertrophy-friendly compounds (heel-elevated squats on a slant board, RDLs, narrow good mornings, hyperextensions), heavy stable split squats as a main lift, reducing leg frequency to twice a week with low volume, and adding hard cardio and weighted carries; isolation is useful but he hasn't needed it.
claims: He reached his goal of 28-inch legs after five years
From 2020-2023 he grew his legs 1 inch while recomping, by finally training his neglected hamstrings with RDLs and hyperextensions
For his first five years he mostly only squatted and never isolated hamstrings, creating a big imbalance
His legs grow quickly as soon as he gains weight; the next inch came while gaining 10 lb
Heavy compounds are king for lower-body hypertrophy, but after a point plain squats and deadlifts give poor returns for the energy spent
Do all squats with elevated heels: more quads, less lumbar involvement, easier recovery
A slant board forces knees forward, a narrow stance and toes forward, which is the way to bigger quads
Heel elevation costs about 15-30% of your squat load, which is good: more stimulus for less fatigue
He uses the board's flatter angle for SSB squats and the steeper first slant for belt and back squats
Plates under the heels are hard to standardize and give little elevation; buy a sturdy, high-quality slant board
Most people misuse the belt squat with wide stance and toes out; on a slant board with feet close your load will be cut in half
200 lb on a heel-elevated belt squat for 15 reps is brutal
Swap deadlifts for Romanian deadlifts: better stretch, eccentric, constant tension on hamstrings and traps
Good mornings for hamstrings: narrow stance, feet forward, shoulders travel past the hips, ideally with an SSB, working up to heavy sets of 12
Hyperextensions: snatch grip for range, don't extend the spine at the top; a barbell under the hip crease plus dumbbells can replicate them
The less knee flexion in a hinge, the more it becomes a pure hinge and the better for hamstrings
Treating split squats or lunges as finishers is poor programming; regard them as heavy main compounds equal to squats
You can build great quads and glutes with only split squats and no squats
Dumbbell split squats are the worst variation: balance limits you around 75-80 lb per hand rather than the muscle
Switching to belt squat and SSB split squats raised his split squat strength about 50% in about 6 months
300 lb per leg on split squats is a realistic hypertrophy goal for a heavy lifter
Always do heavy split squats in a rack with safeties, a Smith machine or a belt squat
Training legs only once a week gives poor work capacity, recovery and constant soreness
Once you squat in the low 400s and RDL in the low 500s, three leg sessions a week becomes unrecoverable
Never sacrifice intensity for frequency; sacrificing frequency for intensity is fine
He now trains legs twice a week (Mon/Thu or Wed/Sat) with 72-96 h between sessions
Progressive overload is king: if lifts go up without much fat gain, you are adding muscle
He keeps upper body three times a week because upper muscles are numerous and recover fast; forearms 3-4x, biceps and chest 2-3x weekly
He does only six sets of quads and six sets of hamstrings/posterior chain per week
Stacking squat, split squat, leg press and leg extension in one session is junk volume
Cardio doesn't kill gains; hard cardio on top of leg training boosts recovery and conditioning
He does cardio twice a week: a hard threshold mile on a non-motorized treadmill pushing off the calves
Stair stepper on tiptoes for 10 minutes with a weighted backpack, now 80 lb, about 300 lb total
On his two days off from the gym he does 30 minutes of weighted carries outdoors
There is no point having big legs if you can't hike or walk without pain; big legs and healthy legs should go together
Muscle built now keeps you mobile in old age
He doesn't do leg isolation because he trains legs at home with no room for machines, and he reached 28 inches without it
Compound-only makes more sense for legs than for arms, which need isolation to maximize each muscle
For a future contest cut and his 30-inch goal he plans to use isolation like leg extensions; his adductors could be bigger
Leg isolation is near-free volume: 3x10-15 leg curls at session end add hamstring stimulus with zero systemic fatigue
Isolation should complement, never replace, compounds, like cable flies can't replace heavy pressing for chest
